contentHtml:
Two customers want slot 42. Ana books through an HTTP API. Ben's booking arrives as a message for a worker. Both call the same Python operation, and PostgreSQL enforces one committed claim per slot. This local reference implementation lets you see the result each caller receives and compare it with the stored reservation.

HTTP client  -> API                    -> reserve() -> slot_claims
producer CLI -> booking_jobs -> worker -> reserve() -> slot_claims
                                worker -> booking_jobs.outcome (same transaction)

The API maps its synthetic bearer token to an actor. The worker and its CLI use a PostgreSQL table as a durable inbox. The worker locks a pending message, calls the shared booking operation and records the outcome in the same transaction as the claim. The queue key is the actor, slot and claim ID. Repeating a delivery with that identity returns the existing job. The schema separately enforces a primary key on the slot in the claims table.

Start and check readiness

Use Docker with Compose supporting up --wait, and curl for the manual HTTP requests. The first build needs access to the base images and Python package index. From the repository root, run the following commands in the same shell.

cd examples/reference-implementations/small-production-service/reservations
docker compose up --build --wait --wait-timeout 90

docker compose ps
api="http://127.0.0.1:${RESERVATION_PORT:-18084}"
curl --noproxy '*' --fail --silent --show-error "$api/ready"

Expect three healthy services and {"ready": true}. The API reads slot 42 from PostgreSQL. The worker health check looks for its polling session in the same database. The contention scenario below verifies actual message processing. Only the API publishes a host port, bound to loopback.

Race the API against the worker

Start with an empty fixture and no other senders. Run the contention scenario from the API container so it can use both the HTTP route and the trusted queue producer.

docker compose exec -T api python scenario.py

The coordinator inserts a provisional claim for slot 42 inside an open transaction. It sends Ana's HTTP request (a1) and enqueues Ben's worker message (b1). Once PostgreSQL reports both application sessions waiting on the coordinator, the coordinator rolls back its claim. The API and worker now compete for the same available slot. The scenario fails if it cannot observe the overlap, if the two outcomes disagree with the contract, or if the row read on a fresh connection disagrees with the winner.

Winner HTTP response to Ana, claim a1 Worker result for Ben, claim b1 Only row in slot_claims
Ana 201 Confirmed SlotTaken 42, ana, a1
Ben 409 SlotTaken Confirmed 42, ben, b1

Inspect the durable worker outcome by its original identity and query the database independently. The result should match one row of the table above.

docker compose exec -T worker python worker.py result ben 42 b1
docker compose exec -T db psql -X -U postgres -d reservations \
  -c 'SELECT slot_id, actor_id, claim_id FROM slot_claims ORDER BY slot_id;'

Reset the fixture and submit the two claims by hand

After all in-flight requests finish, run this reset in the disposable lab. It empties the inbox, its outcomes and the claims in one transaction. It keeps the single parent slot. The scenario checks for an empty fixture at the beginning so a previous run's bookings are visible until you reset them.

docker compose exec -T db psql -X -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -U postgres -d reservations \
  -c 'TRUNCATE booking_jobs, slot_claims;'

The API accepts POST /slots/{slot_id}/claims for an existing slot with a positive integer ID. The default fixture contains only slot 42. An authorized caller requesting an unseeded slot receives HTTP 404 with SlotNotFound.

Submit Ana's claim first. Expect HTTP 201 and a JSON response identifying a1 as Confirmed. Repeating this exact request returns HTTP 200 with the same confirmation. An unauthenticated caller gets 401. The authenticated lab guest (Bearer lab-guest) lacks booking permission and gets 403.

curl --noproxy '*' --silent --show-error --write-out 'HTTP %{http_code}\n' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer lab-ana' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"claim_id":"a1"}' "$api/slots/42/claims"

Deliver Ben's message and look up its outcome. Pending means it is in the inbox. Repeat the read until the worker reports SlotTaken for b1. The worker also logs each terminal result after commit. In this ordering the SQL query above must return precisely 42, ana, a1.

docker compose exec -T worker python worker.py enqueue ben 42 b1
docker compose exec -T worker python worker.py result ben 42 b1

Configuration, persistence and recovery

  • The Compose file runs one database, one API and one worker. Both application processes use the same Dockerfile and a restricted database role. The host operator can administer the lab via Compose. The fixed bearer tokens and default database passwords are public synthetic values for this local exercise.
  • Before startup you can export RESERVATION_PORT to change the host port. Docker allocates the project subnet by default. If its address pool is exhausted, set RESERVATION_SUBNET to an unused private CIDR that does not overlap your Docker networks, host routes or VPN. In the Linux lab shell also export COMPOSE_FILE=compose.yaml:compose.subnet.yaml before running the commands so Compose loads the subnet override.
  • PostgreSQL initializes the role, tables and slot 42 on the first start with an empty named volume. To override the lab passwords, set RESERVATION_APP_PASSWORD and RESERVATION_ADMIN_PASSWORD before this first start. Changing the environment later does not rotate a stored PostgreSQL password.
  • If the worker exits before commit, its booking and inbox update roll back together. Pending jobs survive in the database. An API client that loses its response can retry with the same identity. Inspect docker compose logs worker after a processing failure. Once the database issue is resolved, docker compose up -d worker resumes polling.
  • A single database backs both booking paths and the queue. Loss of its volume loses both reservations and outcomes. The example has no replica or backup and runs on one Docker host. Ingress, production identity, backup/restore and timed deployment recovery need separate controls.

Use docker compose down to stop the project and retain the named volume. To discard all synthetic reservations and remove the lab containers, network and volume, run the following command from this directory.

docker compose down --volumes

The booking contract, reservation schema and two-session integration test give the underlying rule, storage guarantee and database-level exercise. PostgreSQL documents how locking reads can select pending work for a queue and how Read Committed handles conflicting inserts. Locking clauses and transaction isolation.
